author: Carlos Martinez
title: Sleep, hydration, and nutrition for long endurance sim races
description: How to fuel your body and mind for 24-hour and multi-hour iRacing stints without performance loss or fatigue.

sections.p: A 24-hour endurance race in iRacing is a mental and physical test. You sit in the same position for hours. Your focus narrows to lap consistency, fuel management, and track position. By hour eight or twelve, your grip softens, your eyes sting, and your reflexes slip. The difference between a podium finish and an avoidable spin often comes down to whether you prepared your body as carefully as you tuned the setup.

Endurance sim racing demands more than pace. It demands that you show up well-rested, hydrated, and fueled. Most drivers focus only on the race weekend itself, eating whatever is nearby and pushing sleep aside. That is the opposite of race craft. The best approach begins two or three days before the event and carries through to the final hour.

sections.h2: Sleep: the foundation of endurance performance

sections.p: Sleep deprivation kills lap time faster than a loose setup. After six hours without adequate sleep, reaction time drops by 10 to 15 percent. After twelve hours of poor sleep, decision-making becomes unreliable. In a 24-hour race, a mistake born from fatigue costs you not just one lap but potentially the entire race.

Start sleep preparation three days before a major endurance event. Aim for seven to nine hours per night. This is not a bonus, it is the minimum floor. A single night of five or six hours two days before the race creates a sleep deficit your body cannot recover from in time. Night-before cramming does not work for endurance racing any more than it does for an exam.

If the race starts in the evening or night, adjust your sleep schedule three to five days in advance. Sleep one to two hours later each night to shift your circadian rhythm. If you race at 6 p.m. on Friday but normally sleep at 10 p.m., moving bedtime to midnight by Wednesday gives your body time to adapt. Do not try to shift your entire sleep schedule the night before the race.

list: Sleep seven to nine hours per night in the three days leading up to the event.
Adjust your sleep schedule early if the race starts outside your normal waking hours.
Avoid caffeine after 2 p.m. on race day, even if you feel tired during a stint.
Keep your bedroom dark and cool, around 65 to 68 degrees Fahrenheit.
Put your phone away one hour before bed to allow melatonin production.

sections.tip: If you are sharing a 24-hour race with teammates, rotate driver stints so you get at least 4 to 6 hours of sleep during the event. A well-rested teammate performing at 95 percent beats an exhausted solo driver at 60 percent.

sections.p: Dehydration sets in quietly. You do not feel thirsty until you are already 1 to 2 percent dehydrated. At that point, your core temperature rises, your cognitive function slows, and your hands grip the wheel less precisely. A single stint where you forget to drink can cost you half a second per lap. Over a 30-minute race stint, that is three to four seconds lost. In a close race, that is the win.

Water is your primary tool, but water alone does not fully replace what you lose during a long sim racing session. Sweat carries sodium and electrolytes. A three-hour stint can produce 1 to 2 liters of sweat depending on cockpit temperature, rig setup, and how hard you drive. Replacing only water leaves your cells at an osmotic disadvantage and actually increases your fatigue.

Start hydrating the night before the race. Drink 16 to 20 ounces of water two to three hours before you begin. One hour before the race, drink another 8 to 10 ounces. During your stint, sip 4 to 8 ounces every 15 to 20 minutes. This sounds frequent, but small frequent doses are absorbed better than large boluses and do not cause stomach discomfort.

olist: Prepare water bottles or a hydration system the night before. Use a bottle with a wide mouth and a handle so you can grab it quickly between laps or during yellow flags.

For stints longer than 90 minutes, include an electrolyte drink. Sports drinks with 4 to 8 percent carbohydrate concentration (about 6 to 8 grams per 100 milliliters) and 20 to 30 milligrams of sodium per 100 milliliters are the standard. Avoid drinks with more than 10 percent carbs, as they can cause nausea.
Set a timer on your phone or dashboard to remind yourself to drink every 15 to 20 minutes if you tend to forget.
After your stint ends, continue drinking water or electrolyte drink for 30 minutes to rehydrate during your rest period.

sections.p: Avoid alcohol and high-caffeine energy drinks during the race. Alcohol is a diuretic and depletes your hydration reserves. Excessive caffeine (more than 200 to 300 milligrams per session) can increase heart rate and anxiety, which accelerates dehydration and makes your driving less smooth.

Food fuels your brain as much as it fuels your muscles. A long stint taxes your glucose reserves. Blood sugar dips trigger mental fog, poor decision-making, and slower reflexes. You do not need to eat large meals, but you do need to eat consistently and choose foods that sustain energy without causing digestive distress.

Race day meals should begin four to five hours before your first stint. Eat something substantial and balanced: lean protein, complex carbohydrates, and healthy fat. A good example is grilled chicken with brown rice and roasted vegetables, or a salmon fillet with sweet potato and avocado. Aim for 400 to 600 calories and a macronutrient split of roughly 40 percent carbs, 30 percent protein, and 30 percent fat.

Two to three hours before your stint, have a lighter snack. A banana with a tablespoon of almond butter, or a slice of whole grain bread with turkey provides 150 to 200 calories and stabilizes blood glucose without overwhelming your digestive system.

During a stint, do not try to eat a full meal. Your body is focused on driving, not digestion. Instead, consume easily digestible carbohydrates and a small amount of protein. A granola bar, a handful of trail mix, a sports drink, or half a banana are all effective. Aim for 30 to 60 grams of carbohydrates per hour if your stint is longer than two hours, but only if you can eat without losing focus.

list: Eat a balanced meal four to five hours before your first stint (400 to 600 calories).
Have a light snack two to three hours before driving (150 to 200 calories).
During your stint, consume 30 to 60 grams of carbs per hour via granola, bananas, or sports drinks.
Avoid heavy, fatty, or high-fiber foods immediately before and during racing, as they slow digestion and can cause nausea or cramping.
Pack your food the night before so you are not scavenging during the race.

sections.p: Between stints, if you have a two or three-hour break, eat another balanced meal but keep portions moderate. A turkey sandwich with lettuce and tomato, or a bowl of pasta with lean protein works well. This refuels your body and gives your brain something to focus on besides fatigue. After eating, rest for at least 30 minutes before your next stint.

sections.tip: In team endurance racing, designate one person to manage nutrition and hydration for all drivers. Keep snacks and drinks organized in a cooler near the rig. A driver should never have to think about finding water or food during a handover.

sections.h2: The integration: sleep, hydration, and nutrition as a system

sections.p: These three factors do not work in isolation. Poor sleep makes you more sensitive to dehydration. Dehydration impairs your ability to metabolize food and maintain cognitive focus. Poor nutrition combined with inadequate sleep and hydration compounds each other into performance collapse.

The best drivers treat endurance race preparation as a three-day protocol, not a three-hour scramble. Start two days before the event. Sleep well. Hydrate consistently throughout the day, not just during the race. Eat balanced meals at regular times. On race day, follow the same hydration and nutrition schedule you practiced. Do not experiment with new foods, new drinks, or new routines on race day. Your body and mind should feel familiar and stable as you climb into the cockpit.

Over a 24-hour race, the drivers who maintain mental clarity and consistent lap times are almost always the ones who slept eight hours, drank water every 20 minutes, and ate predictable snacks on schedule. That is not flashy. It is not a secret setup file or a new steering technique. It is simply the foundational work that allows your skill to show up when it matters most. A well-built cockpit and tuned car setup do not matter if you are too tired, too thirsty, or too hungry to drive them properly.

faqs.q: How much water should I drink during a three-hour sim racing stint?
faqs.a: Aim for 4 to 8 ounces every 15 to 20 minutes, which totals roughly 36 to 72 ounces (about 1 to 2 liters) over three hours. The exact amount depends on your cockpit temperature, how much you sweat, and your body size. Smaller drivers and cooler cockpits require less; larger drivers and hot setups require more. Start with this range and adjust based on how you feel.

faqs.q: Can I use energy drinks instead of water and electrolyte drinks during endurance racing?
faqs.a: Energy drinks with high caffeine (200 to 300 milligrams or more per serving) can increase heart rate, anxiety, and jitteriness, which accelerates dehydration and makes your driving less smooth. A single energy drink early in your stint for a caffeine boost is acceptable, but do not rely on them throughout. Water and sports drinks with moderate carbs and electrolytes are more sustainable and effective.

faqs.q: What should I do if I start feeling tired during a 24-hour race but I have four hours until my next sleep break?
faqs.a: Stay hydrated and eat a light snack immediately (banana, granola bar, or a sports drink). Fatigue is often a symptom of low blood glucose or dehydration. Take a five-minute walk outside the sim rig if possible to move blood and reset your nervous system. If you must continue driving, focus on smooth inputs and lower target lap times rather than pushing to your maximum. Better to lose one second per lap and stay consistent than to push hard, make a mistake, and lose the race.

faqs.q: Is it okay to skip meals before a long endurance race to avoid stomach issues?
faqs.a: No. Skipping meals causes blood sugar to drop, which impairs focus, reaction time, and decision-making. Instead, eat a balanced meal four to five hours before racing, then a light snack two to three hours before. Avoid heavy, fatty, or high-fiber foods that slow digestion. If you have a sensitive stomach, practice your meal plan during practice sessions weeks in advance so your body adapts before race day.
